rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: Diverse-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhipeng Yi, Xinyu Lin, Minxuan Shan, Zipeng Chen, Yujiao Zhao, Chuanyu Xu, Wenjie Wang
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), where the student generates on its own and a teacher gives a full probability distribution at each position, makes generative recommenders train faster, but the student drifts further and further toward popular items. The bias comes from two places: the teacher's probabilities already favor the SIDs of popular items, and the student rarely generates the SIDs of unpopular items, so those paths get almost no supervision. HERO trains a popular-item teacher and an unpopular-item teacher. Each training example goes to the teacher that matches the group of the item the user actually clicked, and the true SIDs of unpopular items are also sent to the unpopular-item teacher. Only the student is served. In a 15-day A/B test on the Guess What You Like module of the 1688 homepage, GMV rose 3.412%.

papers.title: Large Language Model as Universal Retriever in Industrial-Scale Recommender System
papers.authors: Junguang Jiang, Yanwen Huang, Liu Bin, Xiaoyu Kong, Xinhang Li
papers.summary: Recommendation retrieval is usually split by objective into several channels, such as collaborative retrieval, long-tail retrieval and interest exploration, each with its own data and model. A team at Alibaba's Taobao and Tmall Group finds that one large language model can handle all of them and still beat the dedicated model of each channel. The input states in one sentence what this retrieval is for, and the model directly generates a set of items from tens of millions of candidates, with latency kept within tens of milliseconds. Beyond the offline comparison, on an online advertising platform it raised the core metric, advertising revenue, by 3%. ==One model that switches retrieval objectives on instruction== can save the cost of maintaining many separate channels.

papers.title: Utility-Aware Generative Recommendation: Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes and Utility-Guided Decoding
papers.authors: Yang Hu, Duo Wang, Ning Li, Kang Li, Junda She, Chengcheng Guo, Kuo Cai, Bin Liu, Youhua Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen
papers.summary: Generative recommenders build a video's SID from its content alone, so a video that is often shared and finished and one that is rarely finished get nearly the same code if their content is similar. Beam search then prunes only by generation probability, so high-value candidates can be cut early, and later reranking cannot bring them back. UAGR fixes both ends. A few binary bits in the ID of the last SID token are set aside for the video's value level, graded from post-exposure signals such as shares and completions, and the SID length stays the same. During decoding, each time a token is added, the model uses the current state to predict watch time, shares and similar outcomes. These are weighted into a value score that decides, together with generation probability, which prefixes get pruned. It is fully deployed at Kuaishou and raised video watch time by 0.206%. ==Value has to count at pruning time, not only in later reranking==.

papers.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuosheng Liu, Yihan Wu, Ziyun Xu, Xiaoxuan Liu, Longfei Yun, Kevin Han, Mingze Gao, Pengfei Wang, Junfeng Pan, Wenjie F...
papers.summary: When recommending creators a user does not follow yet, the mainstream approach quantizes creators into SIDs and has a language model generate them, and this paper finds the bottleneck is not the language model but the SID layer. Several creators land on the same SID, and only one can be picked by popularity, so recall is capped and tilted toward creators who are already popular. The quantizer is frozen, so training cannot change the creator representations either. ACT simply gives every creator its own token, trains it end to end, and at inference takes the creators with the highest logits. In a controlled comparison where only the token layer changes, creator-level Recall@15 is 19.8 points higher, and the SID approach's per-user inference latency is about 2.7 times that of ACT. ==With hundreds of thousands of creators, one token each is more direct than SIDs==.

papers.title: PFA: Attention Can Be Progressively Focused in Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Pengjie Zhou, Weiqin Yang, Haibo Xing, Hao Deng, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: The authors at Alibaba found that when a generative recommender decodes with beam search, attention concentrates on a few past behaviors as decoding proceeds, and which behaviors matter stays largely the same from step to step. Building on this, PFA picks the important history once for the whole decode, instead of having every beam pick it again at every step. It attends to the full history as usual at the first decoding step. At the second step it pools the beams' attention over the history, weighted by generation probability, into one shared ranking of important behaviors, and it shrinks the number of kept behaviors by a fixed ratio at each later step. In an online A/B test on an e-commerce ads platform, the user history grew from 128 to 512 behaviors, revenue rose 3.76%. Response time stayed below that of feeding the full history directly.

papers.title: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising
papers.authors: Yatong Xiao, Yibo Sheng, Lixiang Wang, Mingjie Sun, Yunhao Sha, Pengfei Zhang, Shengyu Wang, Peng Wang, Wenjin Wu, Peng ...
papers.summary: Kuaishou made three changes to GR4AD, its deployed generative ad retrieval system, and the result, GR4AD-X, raises online ad revenue by a cumulative 3.07% over GR4AD. All three target the same mismatch: the model picks ads by generation probability, while the platform cares about revenue. The top ten ads by generation probability and the top ten by eCPM barely overlap, with a hit rate of only about 0.02. The first change keeps the two nearest first-level cluster centers for each ad, so it can still be retrieved when one prefix is pruned. The second skips a bigger backbone and instead feeds in twenty-odd extra user-profile and context features from the ranking system and widens the embeddings of key features. The third estimates a revenue value for each SID prefix, namely the mean revenue of the ads beneath it. During pruning, RRF combines each prefix's positions in the probability ranking and in the value ranking into one score, and candidates are cut by that score. ==The changes were stacked one at a time in online tests==.

papers.title: UGR: Unified Generative Ranking for Heterogeneous E-commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Zonghe Shao, Huabin Chen, Sitong Lu, Fangmei Zhu, Yingcai Ma, Ge Fan, Jinguo Gao, Wei Shi, Yanfang Liu, Huiping Chu
papers.summary: Taobao's generative ranking framework UGR has one generative model directly produce the screen the user finally sees. The roughly one thousand organic, ad and other-business candidates of a request go to the model together, and it generates the final list item by item, instead of each business ranking its own items and a blending stage stitching them together. That stitching step is the old problem: the blender inserts other content into the generator's list, positions and context change, and the order the model learned no longer holds. In an online A/B test on Guess You Like, transaction volume rose 3.29%; when the same model ranks only organic items and hands them to the old blender, transaction volume rises only 2.84%, and ==the gap is the value of unified generation itself==.

papers.title: Where Beam Search Loses Top-Ranked Items:First-Step Coverage in Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Heng Yao, Hanwei Zhu
papers.summary: Generative recommenders generate SIDs position by position with beam search, and the usual way to miss fewer good results is to widen every step at once. This paper checks six full test settings of TIGER one by one. Every result that the model's own scores would place in the top 10 but that gets pruned is lost at the very first step. So the better deal is to concentrate width on the first step and narrow the later ones. With this allocation, about half the prefix budget (the total number of prefixes kept across all steps) reproduces the top 10 of a beam search twice as wide, in the same order, with no retraining. ==Beam width should go to the step where results are most easily lost==.

papers.title: Beyond Uniform Token Training: A Multi-Target Framework for Learning Token-Weighted Objectives in Generative Recommenders
papers.authors: Wei-Ning Chiu, Song-Duo Ma, H. Shu, Chuan‐Ju Wang, Pu‐Jen Cheng
papers.summary: Generative recommenders are trained with the same loss weight on every SID token, and this paper finds that weighting tokens by position and rarity reliably improves recommendations. The reason is that the first few positions of an SID decide the broad item group, the later ones only refine it, and some tokens are very rare. This paper adds two kinds of token weights. One looks at position: the more candidate items a position rules out once it is fixed, the larger its weight, so earlier positions weigh more. The other looks at frequency: the less often a token appears in the training data, the larger its weight. During training it optimizes these two weighted losses together with the ordinary likelihood loss. Compared with the base TIGER model, Hit@5 improves 6.11% on average, and both popular and long-tail items get better. ==It only changes loss weights, not the model architecture==, so the cost of adopting it is low.

papers.title: Think Globally, Generate Personally: Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yuxuan Hu, Yingyi Zhang, Wenlin Zhang, Chao Zhang, Haotian Nan, Ziwei Liu, Jiancheng Dong, Tongzhou Wu, Beibei Kong, Lei...
papers.summary: A user's full history and their last few actions describe the same person, but they give different signals. Putting everything into one sequence dilutes the recent interest, while two separate streams fail to line up with each other. MV-Thinker uses one shared set of learnable query vectors with two independent readers to read the full history and the recent history separately. Because both sides use the same queries, their outputs line up one to one while each keeps its own long-term or recent information, and only then does SID generation start. Across four public datasets and two SID construction methods, it beats both discriminative and generative baselines. This is an academic architecture improvement with no online validation yet.

papers.title: Numerical Embeddings for CTR Prediction: A Taxonomy, Unified Benchmark, and Open-Source FuxiCTR Extension
papers.authors: Heng Yao, Hanwei Zhu, Tianying Liu, Yulou Shu, Siyun Hou
papers.summary: There are a dozen or so ways for a CTR model to turn numerical features such as prices and counts into vectors, and in one fair comparison no single method wins everywhere. This used to be hard to compare, because papers differ in preprocessing and training pipelines. This paper puts 18 of them into one codebase with the same tuning budget and compares them across several datasets and backbones. DEER has the best overall rank, but it does not win everywhere: change the dataset or the backbone and the leader can change. When the inputs switch from standardized values back to their original scale, the winner changes in 11 of 27 settings. Accuracy and inference latency also do not rise and fall together. So how to encode numerical features has to be re-tested on your own data and backbone.

papers.title: Improving Ads Ranking Models with Auxiliary Supervision: Techniques and Insights
papers.authors: Nikhil Bhale, Apurva Pathak, SaiSujithKumarReddy MarapaReddy, Xiao Yin, Prateek Bhansali
papers.summary: Ad CVR models are trained on conversion events such as purchases and installs, but conversions are rare: in this Meta model, about half of the training samples have no conversion label. This paper from Meta explains how to fill the gap with other signals. How long a user looks at an ad before clicking, add-to-cart events, the semantics of the ad content and more are trained as auxiliary tasks alongside the main task. At serving time only the main task is used, so there is no extra cost. Auxiliary signals are often noisy. The most effective fix is called LaCo. It combines several auxiliary signals with logic such as AND, OR and NOT, picks the combination that best matches real conversions, especially with the fewest false positives, and trains on it as one new label. It lowers offline NE by 0.25%. After these changes launched together with other improvements, A/B tests showed a significant rise in advertiser conversions. For teams doing conversion prediction, getting the auxiliary labels right matters more than adding more auxiliary tasks.

papers.title: PACT: Defending Recommendation against Promotional News Rewriting via Attack-Diverse Score Consistency
papers.authors: Chongxian Chen, Fan Mo, Xin Fan, Hayato Yamana
papers.summary: News recommendation has a loophole: keep the facts, let an LLM make the headline more sensational, for example by adding words like Thrilling or Ultimate, and the article ranks higher in the list. Existing defenses usually target only one or two rewriting methods. This paper first uses several LLMs and several rewriting strategies to generate, offline, a large pool of fact-checked headline rewrites. During training it samples a few of them each time and asks the model to give the original and the rewritten headline similar scores, while still learning from clicks as usual. At serving time the model architecture is unchanged and there is no extra latency. On three recommendation models on the MIND dataset, facing rewriting models never seen in training, it has the lowest rate of articles pushed up the ranking, up to 3.0 percentage points lower than the strongest defense baseline. The cost is a small drop in ranking metrics for some models.

papers.title: Lightweight Ranking Heads: Accelerating Multi-Task Experimentation in Production Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Sanjay Surendranath Girija, Aniruddh Nath, Li Wei, Yanhao Jiang, Shawn Andrews, Lukasz Heldt, Yi Wu, Aditya Mahajan, Moh...
papers.summary: The bigger a multi-task ranking model gets, the slower it becomes to add a new prediction target. YouTube's answer keeps the new target out of the main model and makes it a small prediction head on top of the shared layers (the paper calls it a Light Head). It only reads the shared layers' output, sends no gradient down, and is reset at the start of every training run, and every ranking model reads it from the same config. With the framework, a full experiment cycle covering the ranker and a downstream model shrank from 24 days to 11. The cost is an AUC about 0.01 lower than a fully trained head on data-rich tasks such as clicks.

papers.title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
papers.authors: Shivam Swarup, Divya Prakash Shrivastava, Rakesh Thakur
papers.summary: Papers on detecting fake shilling accounts in recommender systems usually report a single AUROC. This paper finds that detectors built on model embeddings fail completely under a more realistic attack: the attacker copies a real user's entire item history and slips in only one to three items to promote. On MovieLens-1M, every embedding-based detection score drops to chance. The simplest method works instead: use Jaccard similarity to measure how close each account's item set is to its most similar other account, and AUROC reaches above 0.92. The cause lies in the representation itself. LightGCN's embeddings place a fake account close to the real user it copied, which erases the signal that separates them. So any learned detector should be paired with a similarity check that looks directly at the raw records.

papers.title: BrowseFlow: Sparse Event Flow Matching for Generative User Simulation
papers.authors: Yitian Pang, Jiayi Zhang, Zhenjia Ma, Xiaowei Yue, Dagui Chen, Jian Xu
papers.summary: Shown the same feed, the same user might scroll to item 20 and click two things this time, and leave at item 8 the next; the log keeps only one of these. BrowseFlow argues that a user simulator should learn the distribution of such outcomes rather than copy that one log. It splits a browsing session into two things, how deep the user scrolls and at which positions they click or like, and generates those key events directly instead of predicting a long run of scroll actions step by step. This matters because in Taobao browsing data only 5.48% of actions are positive feedback such as clicks. On three datasets, its generated sessions come closest to real ones both in overall distribution and in click-count distribution.

papers.title: Beyond IPS: Reliable Counterfactual Evaluation in Multi-Stage Ad Systems without Logged Propensities
papers.authors: Mohsen Malmir, Mohamed A. Radwan, Houssam Nassif, Murat Ali Bayir
papers.summary: Before an ad system launches a new ranking model, it must pick the best candidate offline from logs. In multi-stage delivery, impressions pass through auctions, filters and caching, and their selection probabilities are never logged, so IPS cannot be used. The usual substitute scores new policies with a click-predicting reward model, but new policies push impressions toward ads that are rare in the logs, where that model is least accurate. The authors replay the candidates on past requests and train a classifier to tell whether an impression comes from the logs or from a given candidate. For each logged impression, the classifier gives the ratio of its probability under each candidate to its probability under the logs. The average of these ratios over all candidates becomes its weight when training one shared reward model, so impressions that look like what the candidates would show count more. Five candidates in a production CTR ranking system all ran in A/B tests. Picking a winner on each of 50 random log subsamples, the rate of picking the truly best one rises from 0.36 without weighting to 0.40.

papers.title: PRISM: Personalized Item Representations in User History
papers.authors: Renzhi Wu, Zikun Cui, Junjie Yang, Li Sheng, Yongjun Xie, Jerry Fu, Nipun Mathur, Sri Reddy, Hong Li
papers.summary: The same cooking video is a pastime for a casual viewer and source material for a food creator. Yet a recommender gives it the same starting embedding in both users' history sequences. PRISM replaces each history event with a new vector. That vector expresses how this user related to this item at that moment. It reuses the intermediate states of every layer that the upstream ranking model already computed while scoring, and an autoencoder compresses them into one embedding per scored user–item pair. These are stored, and later sequence models read them in time order. On a billion-scale recommendation surface at Meta, downstream NE drops by 0.15% on average. At a similar history length, VISTA, another approach that caches history summaries, drops by only 0.07%. The gain also grows with longer histories. ==The input to a history sequence can itself be personalized==.

papers.title: Read More, Reason Deeper: Latent Workspaces for Long-Sequence Recommendation
papers.authors: Renzhi Wu, Li Sheng, Zikun Cui, Junjie Yang, Tai Guo, Keke Zhai, Yan Li, Jerry Fu, Nipun Mathur, Sri Reddy, Hong Li
papers.summary: This Meta paper gives long-sequence ranking a new structure in which reading more history and stacking more layers become two separately tunable knobs: with 10K history events, its NE beats HSTU by 0.19% while using 69.6% less forward compute. Current models tie the two together. A sequence encoder pays for every extra event in every layer, while models that first select relevant events select only once, so later layers never see what was left out. LWR gives each candidate a small fixed set of vectors as a workspace: some are generated from its features, and some are learned vectors shared by all candidates. Every layer forms queries from the workspace, reads the full history with weights, and uses what it reads to update the workspace for the next layer. ==Reading more and stacking deeper can be scaled separately==.

papers.title: Dynamic Click Destinations: Personalizing Post Ad-Click Landing Experiences
papers.authors: Apurva Pathak, Yuya Shiraki, Iman Jenabzadeh, Nikhil Bhale, Yuwen Tan, Shashank Rangarajan, Amirmehdi Sharifzad
papers.summary: A user taps an offsite ad: should it open the advertiser's website, or jump straight into the advertiser's app already installed on the phone? Switching the default from web to app for everyone actually lowers overall advertiser value (value-weighted conversions) by 1.05%, with a small gain only on ads optimizing for purchases. In other words, which destination is better depends on each click. This paper from Meta picks the destination for each click separately, and the model went through three generations. The last one directly predicts which of the two destinations is better, with training labels taken from the difference between a larger model's conversion scores for the two destinations. In online A/B tests, this generation raises advertiser value by 0.54% over always opening the website. Where a click sends the user is an often overlooked lever for optimization.

papers.title: WeSearch: A Unified Model-Centric Retrieval Framework for WeChat Search
papers.authors: Kepu Zhang, Yuzhe Cai, Yue Shu, Dawei Chen, Jinhai Zhu, Yuan Xu, Zehua Dai, Tongke Ni, Ziyao Chen, Chen Fu, Jie Shao, Ch...
papers.summary: Generative retrieval usually gives each document one fixed hierarchical Semantic ID, which assumes a document follows a single semantic path. Many articles cover several topics at once, so that assumption breaks. WeSearch at WeChat Search changes the order: it first finds the document clusters relevant to the query, then scores individual documents inside those clusters, separating coarse pruning from fine relevance judgment. The index updates incrementally, so the model can be refreshed weekly or even daily. It now serves all WeChat Search traffic, and a month-long full-traffic A/B test showed CTR up 0.68% and retrieval resource cost down 41%. Multi-topic documents no longer have to squeeze into one path.

papers.title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
papers.authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Markus Krimmel, William Barber, Antoine Chaffin, Maximilian Schall, Jonas Golde, Louis Milliken, Ekater...
papers.summary: Contextual embeddings are trained and evaluated as if a question had only one relevant chunk in a document, and this paper shows that assumption fails in RAG. Answering a question often also needs the chunks that say which product or which year the answer is about, yet current training treats every chunk of the same document other than the answer chunk as a negative, so these supporting chunks get pushed down. The authors use an existing context compression model as the teacher. Its normal job is to pick out the parts of a retrieved document relevant to the query, and it gives every token a relevance score. Each chunk's score is the mean of its top few token scores, and the embedding model learns to match it, so no answer-chunk labels are needed. On a new diagnostic benchmark, the 9B model finds the answer in its top 10 chunks for 45.5% of queries, against 31.1% for the strongest baseline, voyage-context-4.

papers.title: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Tiansheng Hu, Yichuan Wang, James V. Talwar, Nicholas Tomlin, Chen Zhao, Sewon Min
papers.summary: Deep research agents that read papers usually OCR each page into text first, and much of the tables, figures and equations is lost at that step. DR Pixel skips the text conversion. It renders 1.06 million paper pages as images and does both retrieval and reasoning directly on the page images. Without any training, this beats the OCR-first pipeline on several of the strongest closed and open models, and it calls tools less often. The authors then fine-tune an open model on teacher trajectories, and give each step its own weight. They remove the step and see how much the final answer quality changes, and the smaller the change, the lower the weight. After training, retrieval recall rises by about 15 points and answer accuracy by more than 10 points. The OCR-then-retrieve step is not just unnecessary, it holds the agent back.

papers.title: Every Clause Counts: Instruction-Following Reranking by Multiplying Small, Answerable Questions
papers.authors: S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed, Abdullah Al Musaddiq
papers.summary: People often attach requirements to search queries, such as pages for beginners, documents in a certain language, or official sources only. Most rerankers were only trained to judge topical relevance, so they treat these requirements as a few extra words. The InfoSearch benchmark measures this with WISE, which gives credit when documents that meet the requirement move up under it and move down under the opposite requirement, with moves near the top counting more. Even GPT-4o used as a reranker averages only 33.5 on WISE. DMReranker splits an instructed query into a topic and a few concrete conditions, has a small model answer one narrow question per condition, and multiplies the probabilities that each condition is met into one score. Nothing is trained, and WISE reaches 50.9. Splitting one complex requirement into several small questions works better than asking a large model to judge the whole sentence at once.

papers.title: Re$^3$Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads
papers.authors: Ruiyi Yan, Zhuoyuan Mao, Yugo Murawaki, Yiwen Guo
papers.summary: Attention-based reranking looks at a few retrieval-focused attention heads in an LLM and measures how much attention they send from the question to each candidate document. But the question is often short and carries few clues. Re3Rank first has the model write a reasoning trace over the question and the candidates, then uses the trace tokens to query those heads, reading the attention each candidate receives as its relevance score. The trace is made of sampled discrete tokens, so gradients cannot flow back. During training, the forward pass scores with the sampled trace as usual, while the backward pass uses the token probabilities from the generator to weight the embeddings, so the ranking loss reaches the part that writes the trace. Across 9 benchmarks it beats the strongest baseline by 3.11 NDCG points on average.

papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
papers.authors: Dingyi Kang, Bingzhe Li
papers.summary: The work that multi-hop question answering piles onto one LLM can be split up. In this paper's DeFT-RAG, the LLM writes one sub-question at a time that names every entity it asks about. A program records each sub-question and its answer in a QA table by fixed rules, and the LLM reads this table at the end to answer the original question. On MuSiQue, accuracy rises from the strongest baseline's 0.577 to 0.629. Because each sub-question names its entities in full, answers can also be reused across questions: 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache and LLM calls drop by 12.9%, with no loss in accuracy. Multi-hop questions are hard because evidence must be found link by link through intermediate entities the question never names. Iterative methods make the LLM plan, order, rewrite and keep track at once, and each task fails in its own way.

papers.title: Decompose, Estimate, Select: Coverage-Aware Context Construction for Long-Form RAG
papers.authors: He Tu, Aleena Bosco Kurumthottam, Torsten Suel
papers.summary: In long-form RAG, more complete retrieval does not necessarily mean a more complete answer. The paper shows this with a retrieval pipeline it builds that computes coverage explicitly. The authors have an LLM split the question into a set of sub-questions, use a cross-encoder to predict which sub-questions each candidate document can answer, and then repeatedly pick the document that answers the most sub-questions not yet covered. On TREC RAG 2024, α-nDCG rises from 0.625 to 0.702, close to the ceiling reached when human-written answer nuggets replace the sub-questions. Yet in a controlled comparison with the generator, candidate pool and document budget fixed, documents chosen directly with the reference labels cover more, but put no more nuggets into the answer. ==Answer completeness depends not only on what is retrieved but also on whether the generator uses it.==

papers.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
papers.authors: Adilet Metinov, Chingiz Arziev
papers.summary: RAG systems usually serve a reranker and a generator side by side, and the candidate passages are read once by each model. Glance starts from the idea that the generator reads these passages anyway, so it may as well rank them. It prefills all candidate passages into the KV cache once and attaches a short scoring prompt for each passage on top of that shared cache. A small set of LoRA weights and a scoring head turn each prompt into a relevance score. Then the LoRA is switched off, and the same model reads the selected passages and writes the answer. Each extra decision skill costs about 0.1 GiB of memory. After brief fine-tuning on MS MARCO, it reaches nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact, against 0.721 for the dedicated reranker bge-reranker-v2-m3. The evaluation covers only two retrieval datasets and one model family, but serving one fewer resident model has a direct effect on serving cost.

papers.title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Chenjie Qiu, Zixuan Zeng, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Dongsheng Luo, Boyan Xu
papers.summary: Chain embedding retrievers for multi-hop retrieval see different histories in training and in use, and this paper fixes that without adding any LLM call. At each step such a retriever joins the question with the passages found so far to look for the next one; in training its history holds only correct passages, but in use it often holds wrong passages it found itself. On four-hop MuSiQue questions, 70% of the retrieval states already contain a wrong passage by the third step. The authors let the current model run on the training questions every epoch and train it on the states it actually reaches, with the earliest still-missing correct passage as the target. With the same recipe, the share of questions whose full evidence is in the top five rises from 44.6% to 50.5%.

papers.title: xPRT: Cross-Passage Retrieval Pretraining
papers.authors: Danush Khanna, Himanshu Singhal, Pranjal A. Chitale, Bishal Santra
papers.summary: Which passages of the same web page talk about related things is, by itself, enough to train a retriever. xPRT first takes passages whose vectors are close enough to the page's mean vector as anchor passages, then, by vector similarity and word overlap, finds for each anchor the four most related passages of the same document. It then trains the embedding: the anchor must pick out its most related passage from candidates mixed with passages of other documents. Once most words of a related passage are masked, a one-layer decoder must use the anchor's vector to fill them back in. Continuing pre-training from the already strong E5 with only the objective changed, five established objectives gain at most 0.38 points on MTEB, while xPRT gains about 1.8 points consistently. ==What matters most is how positives are chosen; the new fill-in term adds only a small part.==

papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
papers.summary: The table in vLLM's documentation that sets how many tokens speculative decoding guesses per step at each batch size can visibly cut throughput on a different GPU or model. This paper gives a tool that measures the best table in minutes and keeps correcting it as traffic changes. Speculation only pays while the GPU has spare compute, so the more requests share a batch, the fewer tokens each step should guess. TableTune times every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and picks the highest-throughput table. Once in production, a plugin reads vLLM's counts of accepted guesses, combines them with the measured step times, and rewrites the table with the length that yields the most useful tokens per second at each batch size. On a mixture-of-experts model, against the fastest fixed draft length at each load, the documented table is up to 18% slower and the measured table at most 3% slower.

papers.title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Huang, Teng Ma, Zhuoran Li, Yibo Zhao, Zhaoshi Li, Qianchao Zhu, Wei Yang, Chenxi Wang, Tao Xie, Youwei Zhuo
papers.summary: After analyzing eight production LLM request traces, the authors find that the common practice of treating host memory as a KV cache layer in front of the SSD barely filters any reads under these workloads. Reused blocks either come back only after a long gap, or belong to agent sessions of several gigabytes each that memory cannot hold, so the SSD always ends up on the read path. FlatCake puts memory and SSD at the same level and decides each block's home when it is created. Shared system prompts and short-reply chats go to memory, while multi-gigabyte agent sessions are written straight to the SSD. A session's blocks are stored contiguously and never move, and reads stream large chunks from the SSD straight into the GPU. Replaying a production Claude Code trace, the share of prefixes it reads back instead of recomputing holds at 94% as load rises, while Mooncake drops to 64%. KV storage for long agent sessions should be planned per session.

papers.title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index
papers.authors: Jeongmin Brian Park, Wen-mei Hwu
papers.summary: In learned sparse attention, as used by DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3, each query attends to only k keys, but the small scoring network that picks those k keys still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, that step takes more than half of prefill time. AttentionIndex sharply cuts this cost. During prefill it groups keys by similarity; a query first scores one representative per group, and only the members of the most promising groups go to the original scoring network for the final pick. At that length, its prefill throughput is 1.3 to 1.8 times that of scoring every key, and it misses fewer keys than HiSA, a block-based method at similar speed.

papers.title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
papers.authors: Hamidreza Alikhani, Nazmul Takbir, Matin Khajavi, Rajat Bhattacharjya, Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi, Nikil Dutt
papers.summary: Prefill queueing under a prefix cache can keep both the median latency low and the tail short. While the queue is short, serve cheap requests with long cache hits first; move a request forward the longer it has waited relative to its own prefill time; and cap how much work cheap requests may place ahead of the oldest request. This is what Fairway does. Agent and RAG requests often share a prefix, so the remaining work of requests in one queue can differ by about 100 times, and the serving order decides how long each request waits for its first token. In traffic spikes, Fairway's median time to first token is 0.82 seconds with a p99 close to first-come-first-served, while hit-leaning orderings let the p99 reach 11 to 50 seconds.

papers.title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs
papers.authors: Dongfang Zhao
papers.summary: For high-recall vector search on GPUs, the fastest graph indexes such as CAGRA walk the graph round by round, each round waiting for the distances of the previous one, and higher recall needs more rounds. OctEx takes another route: it spends GPU memory on neighbor lists computed ahead of time. It makes a few hundred randomly projected low-dimensional copies of the data, each copy assigns vectors to the cells of a regular grid, and for every cell it stores the vectors closest to the cell center. A query reads the lists of its own cells in one step, then reads the stored neighbors of those candidates, in a fixed number of rounds instead of a long chain. On billion-vector datasets on four H100 GPUs, it is 1.46 to 2.05 times faster than CAGRA at high recall. ==Trading GPU memory for serial waiting at query time is the core trade-off of this paper.==

papers.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
papers.authors: Chengzhi Lu, Boxi Zhou, Yanying Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
papers.summary: A ten-minute traffic surge can leave an agent serving engine with prefill and decode disaggregated unable to recover: after the surge ends and traffic returns to a level the engine handled before, goodput on SGLang stays about 88% lower over the following hour. Each agent call resends an ever-longer conversation to the model and relies on prefix caching to skip the recomputation. Behind it is a loop: too little cache causes recomputation, calls slow down, sessions end later, more context is live at once, and the cache falls even shorter. Based on this, the authors build Basin. It predicts the largest context each session will reach over its lifetime, reserves that amount from a total budget that adapts to load, and holds new sessions back when the budget runs out. It reaches 1.20 to 1.70 times the goodput of Continuum. ==This kind of failure shows almost no warning in utilization or queue length.==

papers.title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
papers.authors: Wenhao Chen, Hong Zhang
papers.summary: In LLM serving, running prefill and decode together lets their resource needs complement each other, since prefill uses compute and decode uses memory bandwidth. But the two want different parallelism. A long-prompt prefill must spread across more GPUs to deliver the first token on time, while decode needs only a few. ConfluxServe treats each operator differently. In the linear layers, tokens from both phases form one batch and are computed together under the same weight sharding. At the attention layers they split: decode stays on its own group of GPUs, while prefill spreads across more GPUs through two All-to-All exchanges. Both paths run at the same time and merge back into one batch afterwards. On production workloads, the request rate it sustains within latency targets is 1.26 to 1.62 times that of the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.authors: NVIDIA, Aastha Jhunjhunwala, Aayushi Ashokkumar Srivastava, Abhibha Gupta, Abhinav Garg, Abhinav Khattar, Achsah Wildish...
papers.summary: Open models built for agents often have to choose between capability and inference cost. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super optimizes both. It is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model that activates only about a tenth of its parameters per token, and it scores 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, ahead of the previous-generation Ultra with several times more active parameters. The deployment design matters more to people who serve models. The model carries its own multi-token prediction head for speculative decoding, and post-training trains that head again, raising the average number of accepted tokens per step over the original head by 21.8% when drafts are sampled and by 10.1% under greedy decoding. With NVFP4 quantization, throughput on an interactive agent workload is 2.43 times that of BF16. Base, post-trained and quantized weights are released together with the training data.

papers.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Fang, Dingyang Li, Jianfeng Zhong, Bin Wang, Weixi Zhu, Cunshu Ni, Zicong Hong, Wuhui Chen, Zibin Zheng
papers.summary: Putting an MoE model's expert weights and its KV cache into one shared pool of GPU memory, and shifting how much each side gets as load changes, lets a memory-limited machine serve many more concurrent requests. Rimuru is a serving system built this way. When requests pile up, it moves rarely used experts out of GPU memory to free pages for the KV cache, and when traffic drops, it brings experts back. To make this work, it rewrites the MoE kernel to read expert weights that are not stored contiguously. Existing expert-offloading systems split GPU memory into two fixed regions at startup, so the KV cache runs short as soon as requests pile up. On 5090 machines whose GPU memory just fits all the weights, Rimuru moves some experts out on purpose to admit more requests, and its throughput is 1.1 to 2.88 times that of vLLM and SGLang, which keep all weights in GPU memory.

papers.title: SGLang security update: improving request isolation
papers.authors: SGLang Team
papers.summary: In one of Cloudflare's production model deployments, a request received content from another user's session. The SGLang team traced it to the path where prefill and decode run on separate workers. A request that exceeded the prefill KV cache capacity should have been rejected, yet it still went through the handoff, and decode read cache pages that had never been filled for it. They also fixed a related hazard. When a request is interrupted midway, RDMA writes already sent are still in flight, but decode had already returned the destination slots to the allocator, so the late data could land in another request's KV cache without any error. The fix releases the slots only after those writes are confirmed to have landed. On two H100 GPUs, throughput before and after the fix differs by less than 2%. Teams running disaggregated serving should upgrade and check that context length matches cache pool capacity.

papers.title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
papers.authors: Zhixuan Xu, Yichen Li, Bingchen Wu, Rui Wang, Yiwen Hou, Zixuan Liu, Tianyu Qiu, Lin Shao
papers.summary: Teaching a robot hand from human demonstrations is hard because human and robot hands have different shapes. If the conversion only tries to make the robot hand look like the human hand, the robot's fingertips often touch the object in different places than the human did, and grasps and pushes fail. CIMI puts contact first. During demonstrations it records the contact surfaces between fingers and object plus fingertip camera views; when converting to robot motion it aligns the contact points first and the finger pose second. The learned policy likewise predicts how the contact surface should move next, and a controller coordinates wrist and fingers to match it. Across six hand-task pairs on the LEAP and Wuji hands, mean full-task success beats baseline policies by at least 50 percentage points. ==When transferring human skills, matching contact matters more than matching hand shape==.

papers.title: LeRobot:  An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
papers.authors: Remi Cadene, Simon Alibert, Francesco Capuano, Michel Aractingi, Adil Zouitine, Pepijn Kooijmans, Jade Choghari, Martino...
papers.summary: The robot learning toolchain is fragmented: motor communication, data collection, dataset formats, training algorithms and deployment each tend to use their own stack, so switching robots or datasets means re-assembling everything, and other people's results are hard to reproduce. LeRobot puts the whole chain into one open-source library: low-level motor control and support for low-cost hardware, a unified dataset format with streaming, implementations of several mainstream policy algorithms, and asynchronous inference. Its value is not a new algorithm but letting data and results from different labs be compared and reused within one set of tools.

papers.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
papers.authors: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang, Amish Sethi
papers.summary: Most of the training data came from handheld grippers, collected at a different place and under different lighting than the test scene, with only a small share of real-robot teleoperation. Fine-tuned on this mix, pi0.5 succeeded in all 10 trials of a bimanual task that puts oranges into a bowl. The demonstrations come from UMI-Live, an open-source bimanual handheld data-collection system released with the paper. The camera, LiDAR, compute and battery are packed into the gripper, the operator presses one button to record the next take, and a background pipeline turns finished takes into training-ready data. ==UMI-Live's value is not a new algorithm but a data-collection pipeline you can actually reproduce==, and the authors also release about 40 hours of data.

papers.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
papers.summary: A low validation loss does not mean an imitation-learning policy works on the real robot. The authors had a five-fingered robot hand grasp and insert an RJ45 network connector and tested 281 policies on hardware to find which design choices actually decide success. The answer: how observations and actions are represented matters far more than the optimizer or sampling scheme. For point-cloud policies, keeping only the region around the target and expressing the points in the robot-base frame each raised success by 70 to 100 percentage points. Among dozens of offline metrics, only a few measuring whether predicted motion is smooth and direct correlated clearly with insertion success, and only within a single policy family. ==Offline metrics cannot yet replace real-robot testing==.

papers.title: ReGATE: Recurrent Gated Visual Fusion for Reactive Humanoid-Object Interaction
papers.authors: Hao Zhu, Jorge Peña-Queralta
papers.summary: When a humanoid robot reaches for a box, the box blocks its head depth camera as soon as the hands get close, yet the controller still has to finish the whole sequence of picking up, carrying and putting down. This paper lets the robot act mainly through the joint-state pathway and treats the depth image only as a correction scaled by learned gates, designed to let less of it in when the image is unreliable. Information gathered over earlier frames is kept in the memory of recurrent layers, so it is not lost the moment the image drops out. In simulation it picks up static boxes 85.2% of the time, against 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol. On a real Unitree G1, after the camera saw the box once and was then completely covered, the robot still grasped the box. ==When the view can be blocked, relying mainly on joint states and taking in the image as needed is steadier.==

papers.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
papers.authors: Adrian B. Ghansah, Yujin An, Jeeseop Kim, Soon-Jo Chung
papers.summary: Getting a humanoid to sprint, walk backwards, sidestep, spin in place and hop on one leg usually means preparing reference trajectories or training a separate policy for each behaviour. FORGE does it in two stages. First it trains a reference generator on a simplified body model: forces are computed as if the whole body were one rigid body, while joint poses follow the full robot, and it produces whole-body reference motions in real time from velocity commands. Then it freezes the generator and trains a second policy to track those references on the full robot dynamics. On a Unitree G1, one generator plus one tracking policy covers forward speed of 2.8 metres per second, backward speed of 2 metres per second, one-legged hopping, and smooth switching between these commands. Because the simplified model is cheap to compute, references can be generated online over a wide range of commands.

papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
papers.summary: For a task like the Tower of Hanoi, where a robot must chain many moves, planning with a visual world model tends to drift further off the longer it plans. VQ-WM compresses images into a finite set of discrete states, searches for the shortest path to the goal over those states, then has a controller with visual feedback walk the path segment by segment. The key is how the discrete states are chosen. Instead of clustering by embedding distance, it runs the controller inside the learned world model, and records how many calls it takes to get from each state to a candidate state. It then picks as few candidates as possible so that every state in the data can reach one of them within a few calls. That way every step on the path is within the controller's reach. Trained only on short play data, it reaches 100% task progress on the physical Tower of Hanoi, while existing foundation models such as VLAs succeed only when the full solution happens to be in their training data.

papers.title: Catch It All!: Generalizable Dynamic Catching with a Dexterous Hand
papers.authors: Arth Shukla, Kehlani Fay, Huaze Liu, Darin Djapri, Alexiy Buynitsky, Nicklas Hansen
papers.summary: Catching thrown objects is hard for a humanoid because objects differ so much: plush toys barely bounce, chip bags deform, hard balls rebound on contact, and a humanoid's wrist torque is small enough that overly aggressive motions can damage the hardware. The authors train a reinforcement learning policy only in simulation on simple shapes. Its grasp reward is based on the distance from the fingertips to the object surface, so the closer the fingers wrap the object the higher the reward. A penalty on exceeding rated torque grows over training, so the policy learns to stay within limits. They then deploy it on a Unitree G1 with no real-robot data, using a single camera from the robot's own viewpoint. On objects never seen in training, underhand catches, palm up and low, succeed 38.9% of the time, and overhand catches, hand raised high, succeed 36.1%, while an expert teleoperator manages only 6.8% on the same task. Motions this fast cannot be captured well by teleoperation, so reinforcement learning in simulation is the more realistic route.

papers.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
papers.authors: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang, Stef Ren, Jianwen Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, ...
papers.summary: Mobile manipulation policies trained on offline demonstrations tend to fail as soon as they meet situations not seen in training, and for long tasks where arm, torso and base must move together, recording more demonstrations cannot cover everything. I3L lets an operator take over when the robot goes wrong. The operator has a pair of leader arms that move in sync with the robot's arms, plus a pair of handheld controllers. Gripping a leader arm or pushing a controller hands full control to the person, who corrects the arms with the leader arms and steers torso and base with the controllers. The corrections are used for retraining, the new policy goes back on the robot, and the next round targets its new mistakes. After four rounds, autonomous success is on average 68.3 percentage points above the initial policy. With the same number of training trajectories it beats demonstration-only training by 35.6 points. ==Spending the demonstration budget where the policy actually fails beats recording more evenly==.

papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: Collective Experience Learning Across 96 Robots
papers.authors: Chao Yu, Shu'ang Yu, Hao Lin, Hongzhi Zang, Yuxiang Yan, Chenxi Jiang, Zhen Guo, Chuankang Li, Yihao Chen, Xin Xu, Xu Fu...
papers.summary: Deployed robots work every day, but improving their policy usually still requires experts to demonstrate or correct actions, which scales poorly as fleets grow. This paper lets a fleet learn from its own execution records: operators only label each episode as success or failure and reset the scene. During training, the context of each failure is used to retrieve similar segments from successful trajectories, whose recorded actions are prioritized for imitation, and the updated shared policy is sent back to every robot. With collection time per robot held fixed, more robots generally means better results; on multi-stage phone packaging, learning across 96 robots raised success from 79.2% to 98.3%. ==Without extra expert demonstrations, success-or-failure labels alone can keep a whole fleet improving==.
